records.source: וַיַּֽעֲמֹ֥ד שָׂטָ֖ן עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיָּ֨סֶת֙ אֶת־דָּוִ֔יד לִמְנ֖וֹת אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And stood up Satan against Israel, and incited David to count Israel.
pieces: Satan rose up against Israel and stirred David up to count Israel.

L.1: And Satan stood up against Israel and incited David to count Israel.

R.1: Satan came against Israel. He moved David to count the people of Israel.

decisions.choice: Satan: the adversary who opposes God's people, here without the article and read as a name
alternatives: an adversary: an opponent, not named, who stood against Israel
the accuser of Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3, not yet used as a personal name
decisions.reason: The word means "adversary" or "accuser". In Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1-2 it has the article, "the adversary", a figure who stands in Yahweh's heavenly court and accuses. Here it has no article. That may mean it is used as a name, Satan, or that it means simply "an adversary", as it does of the human enemies Yahweh raised up against Solomon (1 Kings 11:14, 23, 25) and of the angel of Yahweh who stood in Balaam's way (Numbers 22:22). The verb "incited" is the one used of the adversary in Job 2:3. The text does not settle which is meant; this translation reads it as the name.

decisions.choice: 1 Chronicles 21:1-27 retells 2 Samuel 24:1-25; here an adversary, not the anger of Yahweh, incites David
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:1 begins: "Again the anger of Yahweh burned against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, Go, count Israel and Judah." The Chronicler uses the same verb "incited" but names Satan as the one who stood against Israel. The two accounts look at one event from two sides: Scripture elsewhere speaks of God carrying out judgment through a hostile agent (1 Samuel 16:14; 1 Kings 22:19-23; see the note at 2 Samuel 24:1). This verse also leaves out "again" and has the plain "to count Israel" for David's spoken command. Each record of this chapter notes where its words differ from 2 Samuel 24.

decisions.choice: stood up against: took a stand as an opponent
decisions.reason: The verb means to stand or rise; with "against" it describes someone taking a position as an enemy. The adversary acts against Israel, and he does it by moving its king to sin.

decisions.choice: Satan
decisions.reason: Every level gives the word as a name, with a capital, since it has no article. The footnote gives "an adversary" as the other way to read it.

decisions.choice: stirred David up (Balanced); moved David (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:1. Readable also says "the people of Israel", as there.

records.heading: David counts Israel

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר דָּוִ֤יד אֶל־יוֹאָב֙ וְאֶל־שָׂרֵ֣י הָעָ֔ם לְכ֗וּ סִפְרוּ֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל מִבְּאֵ֥ר שֶׁ֖בַע וְעַד־דָּ֑ן וְהָבִ֣יאוּ אֵלַ֔י וְאֵדְעָ֖ה אֶת־מִסְפָּרָֽם׃
records.gloss: And said David to Joab and to [the] commanders of the people, Go, count Israel from Beer-sheba and to Dan, and bring [it] to me, and I will know their number.
pieces: David told Joab and the troop commanders, "Go and count Israel from Beersheba to Dan, then bring me the report, so that I may know how many there are."

L.2: And David said to Joab and to the commanders of the people, "Go, count Israel from Beersheba to Dan, and bring [the report] to me, so that I may know their number."

R.2: So David said to Joab and the army commanders, "Go and count the people of Israel, from Beersheba in the far south to Dan in the far north. Then bring me the report, so that I will know how many there are."

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:2
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:2 has "the king" where this verse has "David", speaks to Joab alone as "the commander of the army who was with him", and tells him to "go about through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and register the people". Here the commanders are addressed together with Joab (in 2 Samuel 24:4 they go out with him), the verb is the ordinary word for counting, the land is named from south to north, and David adds "bring it to me".

decisions.choice: from Beersheba to Dan: the whole land, named from south to north
decisions.reason: Beersheba was the southernmost town of Israel and Dan the northernmost. 2 Samuel 24:2 names them from north to south; the Chronicler names them from south to north, as in 2 Chronicles 30:5. The sense is the same: the whole country.

decisions.choice: the commanders of the people: the officers of the army
decisions.reason: "The people" here means the people as an army, as often in Samuel and Chronicles (2 Samuel 18:1). These are the officers who carry out the count with Joab (2 Samuel 24:4).

decisions.choice: bring [the report] to me; bring me the report
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "bring to me", with no object. What is to be brought is the result of the count (verse 5).

decisions.choice: the troop commanders (Balanced); the army commanders; in the far south ... in the far north (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "troops" and "army" for "the people" as an army. Readable says where the two towns lay, as at 2 Samuel 24:2.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֗ב יוֹסֵף֩ יְהוָ֨ה עַל־עַמּ֤וֹ׀כָּהֵם֙ מֵאָ֣ה פְעָמִ֔ים הֲלֹא֙ אֲדֹנִ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ כֻּלָּ֥ם לַאדֹנִ֖י לַעֲבָדִ֑ים לָ֣מָּה יְבַקֵּ֥שׁ זֹאת֙ אֲדֹנִ֔י לָ֛מָּה יִהְיֶ֥ה לְאַשְׁמָ֖ה לְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And said Joab, May add Yahweh to his people as they [are] a hundred times; [are they] not, my lord the king, all of them to my lord as servants? Why does seek this my lord? Why should it be as guilt for Israel?
pieces: But Joab said, "May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} make {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people a hundred times as many as they are! Are they not all, my lord the king, servants of my lord? Why does my lord wish for this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?"

L.3: And Joab said, "May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} add to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people a hundred times as many as they [are]! My lord the king, are they not all my lord's servants? Why does my lord seek this? Why should it become [a cause of] guilt for Israel?"

R.3: But Joab answered, "I pray that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will make {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people a hundred times more than they are now! My king, all of them are already your subjects. Why do you want to do this? Why should you bring guilt on Israel?"

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:3
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:3 has "Yahweh your God", "the people", the doubled "as they are and as they are", and the wish "while the eyes of my lord the king see it"; it asks why the king "delights in" this thing. Here Joab says "his people", adds the question "are they not all my lord's servants?", uses the verb "seek", and ends with a second question that 2 Samuel does not have: why should this bring guilt on Israel?

decisions.choice: guilt: guilt that makes the people liable to punishment
decisions.reason: The word names a wrong together with the liability it brings, as when a priest's sin brings guilt on the people (Leviticus 4:3). Joab sees that the king's census will make all Israel answerable for it, and so it does (verse 7).

decisions.choice: are they not all my lord's servants?: a question that expects "yes"
decisions.reason: Joab's point is that the people already belong to the king. Counting them adds nothing to what he has; only Yahweh can increase them.

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: The word, which can mean "slave", here names the king's subjects, as it names a king's officials elsewhere; the whole people are his to command. Literal and Balanced say "servants", as for the king's officials; Readable says "subjects".

decisions.choice: My king, all of them are already your subjects; Why should you bring guilt on Israel?
decisions.reason: Joab speaks of the king in the third person, as a courtier did. Readable lets him speak to David directly, turns the first question into the statement it implies, and says "subjects" for the king's people.

records.source: וּדְבַר־הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ חָזַ֣ק עַל־יוֹאָ֑ב וַיֵּצֵ֣א יוֹאָ֗ב וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ֙ בְּכָל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיָּבֹ֖א יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם׃
records.gloss: And [the] word of the king prevailed against Joab; and went out Joab and went about through all Israel, and came [to] Jerusalem.
pieces: But the king's order overruled Joab, so Joab went out and traveled through all Israel, and then came back to Jerusalem.

L.4: But the king's word prevailed against Joab. So Joab went out and went about through all Israel, and came to Jerusalem.

R.4: But the king would not change his order, even though Joab was against it. So Joab left and went all through Israel. Then he came back to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: a short form of 2 Samuel 24:4-8
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:4 says the king's word prevailed "against Joab and against the commanders of the army", and 24:5-8 traces their route around the land, from Aroer east of the Jordan north to Dan and Sidon, then south to Beersheba, ending in Jerusalem "at the end of nine months and twenty days". The Chronicler names only Joab and gives the whole journey in one line.

decisions.choice: the king's word prevailed against Joab: the king overruled him
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:4. The verb means "was strong against": the king's command won over Joab's objection.

decisions.choice: came back
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:8. Joab set out from Jerusalem, so Balanced and Readable say he came back.

decisions.choice: would not change his order, even though Joab was against it
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:4: Readable spells out what "prevailed against" implies.

records.source: וַיִּתֵּ֥ן יוֹאָ֛ב אֶת־מִסְפַּ֥ר מִפְקַד־הָעָ֖ם אֶל־דָּוִ֑יד וַיְהִ֣י כָֽל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֡ל אֶ֣לֶף אֲלָפִים֩ וּמֵאָ֨ה אֶ֤לֶף אִישׁ֙ שֹׁ֣לֵֽף חֶ֔רֶב וִֽיהוּדָ֕ה אַרְבַּע֩ מֵא֨וֹת וְשִׁבְעִ֥ים אֶ֛לֶף אִ֖ישׁ שֹׁ֥לֵֽף חָֽרֶב׃
records.gloss: And gave Joab [the] number of the registration of the people to David; and was all Israel a thousand thousands and a hundred thousand men drawing [the] sword, and Judah four hundred and seventy thousand men drawing [the] sword.
pieces: Joab gave David the total of the people who had been registered: in all Israel there were 1,100,000 men who could handle a sword, and in Judah 470,000 men who could handle a sword.

L.5: And Joab gave the number of the registration of the people to David. And all Israel was 1,100,000 men who drew the sword, and Judah [was] 470,000 men who drew the sword.

R.5: Joab gave David the results of the count. In all Israel there were 1,100,000 men who could fight with a sword. In Judah there were 470,000 men who could fight with a sword.

decisions.choice: 1,100,000 in all Israel and 470,000 in Judah: the figures of this account
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:9, telling the same story, gives 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah. 1 Chronicles 27:24 says that Joab began the count but did not finish it, and the next verse here says that Levi and Benjamin were left out. The two accounts may count different groups ("all Israel" here may take in more than the "Israel" of 2 Samuel), or the numbers may have been changed in copying; the text does not explain the difference.

decisions.choice: thousand: the ordinary number word
decisions.reason: As at 2 Samuel 24:9 and in the census lists of Numbers (see the note at Numbers 1:21), the word is read as the number "thousand", though it can also name a military or clan unit, which would give smaller numbers.

decisions.choice: men who drew the sword: men fit for battle
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:9, which adds "men of strength". The phrase describes men who could be called up to fight (Judges 8:10; 20:2).

decisions.choice: men who could handle a sword (Balanced); men who could fight with a sword (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:9. Balanced and Readable keep the repeated phrase for Judah, as the Hebrew does.

records.source: וְלֵוִי֙ וּבִנְיָמִ֔ן לֹ֥א פָקַ֖ד בְּתוֹכָ֑ם כִּֽי־נִתְעַ֥ב דְּבַר־הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֶת־יוֹאָֽב׃
records.gloss: And Levi and Benjamin not he registered among them, for abhorrent was [the] word of the king to Joab.
pieces: But Levi and Benjamin he left out of the count, for Joab found the king's order hateful.

L.6: But Levi and Benjamin he did not register among them, for the king's word was abhorrent to Joab.

R.6: But Joab did not count the tribes of Levi and Benjamin, because he hated the king's order.

decisions.choice: Levi and Benjamin not counted: a detail not in 2 Samuel 24
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24 says nothing of tribes left out. 1 Chronicles 27:24 says Joab began to count but did not finish. The law kept Levi out of the census of fighting men (Numbers 1:47-49), so leaving Levi out followed the law. The text does not say why Benjamin was left out, beyond Joab's dislike of the order.

decisions.choice: abhorrent: loathsome, detestable
decisions.reason: The verb is a strong one, used of what is disgusting or detestable. Joab, who had objected (verse 3), carried out the order but did not do all of it.

decisions.choice: Joab; the tribes of
decisions.reason: Readable names Joab as the one who did not count and calls Levi and Benjamin tribes.

records.source: וַיֵּ֨רַע֙ בְּעֵינֵ֣י הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים עַל־הַדָּבָ֖ר הַזֶּ֑ה וַיַּ֖ךְ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ
records.gloss: And was evil in [the] eyes of God concerning this thing, and he struck Israel.
pieces: God was displeased with this thing, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} struck Israel.

L.7: And this thing was evil in the eyes of God, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} struck Israel.

R.7: God was not pleased with what David had done, so {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} punished Israel.

decisions.choice: God was displeased and struck Israel: a verse not in 2 Samuel 24
decisions.reason: In 2 Samuel 24:10 it is David's own heart that "struck him" after the count, and he confesses before any word comes from God. Here God's displeasure comes first, and the same verb "struck" is used of what God does to Israel. David's confession follows in verse 8.

decisions.choice: he struck Israel: a summary of the judgment told in verses 14-15
alternatives: a first blow, before the plague, that led David to confess
decisions.reason: The plague itself is told after David's choice (verse 14). This short clause likely states in advance what the rest of the story tells in full. It could also describe a first blow, before the plague, that made David see his sin.

decisions.choice: was evil in the eyes of God: was displeasing to God
decisions.reason: "In the eyes of" means in someone's judgment. The census was wrong in God's sight.

decisions.choice: was displeased with (Balanced); was not pleased with what David had done; punished (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the idiom in plain words. Readable says what "this thing" was and says "punished" for "struck".

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִיד֙ אֶל־הָ֣אֱלֹהִ֔ים חָטָ֣אתִֽי מְאֹ֔ד אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשִׂ֖יתִי אֶת־הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה וְעַתָּ֗ה הַֽעֲבֶר־נָא֙ אֶת־עֲו֣וֹן עַבְדְּךָ֔ כִּ֥י נִסְכַּ֖לְתִּי מְאֹֽד׃פ
records.gloss: And said David to God, I have sinned greatly that I have done this thing; and now, take away, please, [the] iniquity of your servant, for I have acted foolishly exceedingly.
pieces: Then David said to God, "I have sinned greatly by doing this. Now please take away {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} servant's guilt, for I have acted very foolishly."

L.8: And David said to God, "I have sinned greatly in that I have done this thing. And now, please take away the iniquity of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} servant, for I have acted very foolishly."

R.8: Then David said to God, "I have done a very sinful thing. Now please take away my guilt. I have been very foolish."

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:10
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:10 opens with "David's heart struck him after he had counted the people" and has David speak to "Yahweh", calling on him by name a second time ("and now, Yahweh, take away ..."). Here David speaks to "God", with no name in the plea, and says "in that I have done this thing" for "in what I have done". The rest is the same.

decisions.choice: take away the iniquity: remove the guilt and its punishment
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:10. The word for iniquity covers both the wrong and the guilt it brings.

decisions.choice: your servant: a humble way of saying "I"
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:10: speaking to a superior, a person called himself "your servant".

decisions.choice: your servant (Literal, Balanced); my (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:10: Literal and Balanced keep the polite form; Readable says "my guilt", which is what it means.

records.source: וַיְדַבֵּ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־גָּ֔ד חֹזֵ֥ה דָוִ֖יד לֵאמֹֽר׃
records.gloss: And spoke Yahweh to Gad, [the] seer of David, saying,
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to Gad, David's seer:

L.9: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to Gad, David's seer, saying,

R.9: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to Gad, who was David's seer, a prophet who brought David messages from God. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Gad,

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:11
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:11 begins "And David rose in the morning" and says that "the word of Yahweh came to Gad the prophet, David's seer". Here Yahweh simply "spoke" to Gad, with no time given and no title "the prophet". The word for "seer" is the same in both.

decisions.choice: Gad, David's seer: a prophet who served at David's court
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:11. Gad was with David from his years as a fugitive (1 Samuel 22:5), and 1 Chronicles 29:29 names him among those who recorded David's history. "Seer" is an older title for a prophet, one to whom God shows things.

decisions.choice: a prophet who brought David messages from God; The LORD said to Gad
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:11: Readable explains "seer" the first time it appears in this chapter and names the speaker of the next verse.

decisions.choice: a colon in place of "saying"
decisions.reason: Balanced introduces the message with a colon, since it begins in the next verse.

records.heading: Gad brings David three choices

records.source: לֵךְ֩ וְדִבַּרְתָּ֨ אֶל־דָּוִ֜יד לֵאמֹ֗ר כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה שָׁל֕וֹשׁ אֲנִ֖י נֹטֶ֣ה עָלֶ֑יךָ בְּחַר־לְךָ֛ אַחַ֥ת מֵהֵ֖נָּה וְאֶֽעֱשֶׂה־לָּֽךְ׃
records.gloss: Go and speak to David, saying, Thus says Yahweh: Three [things] I [am] holding out over you; choose for yourself one of them, and I will do [it] to you.
pieces: "Go and tell David, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: I am offering you three things. Choose one of them, and I will do it to you.'"

L.10: "Go and speak to David, saying, 'Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Three [things] I am holding out to you. Choose for yourself one of them, and I will do [it] to you.'"

R.10: "Go and tell David, 'This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: I am giving you three choices. Choose one of them, and I will do it to you.'"

decisions.choice: holding out: a different verb from 2 Samuel 24:12
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:12 has a verb meaning "lay on": three burdens laid on David. Here the verb means to stretch out or hold out, so the three are held out for David to choose from. This verse also adds "saying" before the message. Otherwise the words are the same.

decisions.choice: choose one of them: the punishment is certain, its form is left to David
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:12. Yahweh does not let the sin pass, but he lets David choose how the punishment will come.

decisions.choice: double quotes for Yahweh's words to Gad, single quotes for the message to David
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:12: Gad is to pass on Yahweh's words, so they stand as a quotation inside Yahweh's own speech.

decisions.choice: offering you three things (Balanced); giving you three choices (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state the sense of "holding out three over you" in natural English.

records.source: וַיָּ֥בֹא גָ֖ד אֶל־דָּוִ֑יד וַיֹּ֥אמֶר ל֛וֹ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה קַבֶּל־לָֽךְ׃
records.gloss: And came Gad to David and said to him, Thus says Yahweh: Take for yourself:
pieces: So Gad went to David and said to him, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: 'Take your choice:

L.11: So Gad came to David and said to him, "Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: 'Take for yourself:

R.11: So Gad went to David and told him, "This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: 'Choose one of these:

decisions.choice: Gad gives the choices as Yahweh's own words: a difference from 2 Samuel 24:13
decisions.reason: In 2 Samuel 24:13 Gad "told him, and said to him", and put the three choices to David as questions in his own words. Here he opens with "Thus says Yahweh" and passes on the offer as Yahweh's speech, as Yahweh told him to (verse 10).

decisions.choice: take for yourself: accept one, take your pick
decisions.reason: The verb means to receive or accept. With "for yourself" it invites David to take whichever of the three he will. It is the same offer as "choose for yourself" in verse 10.

decisions.choice: double quotes for Gad's speech, single quotes for Yahweh's words; neither closed here
decisions.reason: Gad's speech runs into verse 12. The words he passes on from Yahweh close in verse 12 before his own closing question, and his speech closes at the end of that verse.

records.source: אִם־שָׁל֨וֹשׁ שָׁנִ֜ים רָעָ֗ב וְאִם־שְׁלֹשָׁ֨ה חֳדָשִׁ֜ים נִסְפֶּ֥ה מִפְּנֵי־צָרֶיךָ֮ וְחֶ֣רֶב אוֹיְבֶ֣ךָ׀לְמַשֶּׂגֶת֒ וְאִם־שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת יָ֠מִים חֶ֣רֶב יְהוָ֤ה וְדֶ֨בֶר֙ בָּאָ֔רֶץ וּמַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֔ה מַשְׁחִ֖ית בְּכָל־גְּב֣וּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְעַתָּ֣ה רְאֵ֔ה מָֽה־אָשִׁ֥יב אֶת־שֹׁלְחִ֖י דָּבָֽר׃פ

And now consider what I shall return [to] the one sending me [as a] word.
pieces: three years of famine; or three months of being swept away by your foes, with the sword of your enemies catching up with you; or three days of the sword of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, a plague in the land, with the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} bringing destruction throughout all the territory of Israel.' Now decide what answer I should take back to the one who sent me."

L.12: either three years of famine, or three months of being swept away before your foes while the sword of your enemies overtakes [you], or three days of the sword of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, pestilence in the land, with the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} destroying throughout all the territory of Israel.' And now consider what word I shall return to the one who sent me."

R.12: three years of famine; or three months of being swept away by your enemies, as their swords catch up with you; or three days when {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will strike with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own sword. That would be a deadly plague in the land, with the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} bringing death all through Israel.' Think about it and decide. Then tell me what answer I should give to the one who sent me."

decisions.choice: three years of famine: the figure in Chronicles
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:13, in the same story, reads "seven years" in the Hebrew, while the ancient Greek translation there reads "three years", as here. Three fits the pattern of the offer: three years, three months, three days. The difference probably arose in copying (see the note at 2 Samuel 24:13).

decisions.choice: the second and third choices are told more fully than in 2 Samuel 24:13
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:13 has "three months of your fleeing before your foes while they pursue you" and "three days of pestilence in your land". Here the enemies' choice is "being swept away", with their sword overtaking David, and the third choice is "the sword of Yahweh", a pestilence carried out by "the angel of Yahweh destroying" through the whole land. In 2 Samuel the angel first appears in 24:16. The closing words are also shorter: 2 Samuel has "know and see", this verse only "see", that is, "consider".

decisions.choice: the sword of Yahweh: Yahweh's own judgment, set against the sword of the enemy
decisions.reason: David may fall by the sword of his enemies or by Yahweh's sword. The second is the pestilence, which the next words describe as the work of a destroying angel, as at the Passover in Egypt (Exodus 12:23). David will see the angel's sword in verse 16.

decisions.choice: being swept away: being destroyed, carried off
decisions.reason: The verb means to sweep away or snatch away, and is used of being destroyed in a disaster (Genesis 19:15, 17). It is stronger than the "fleeing" of 2 Samuel 24:13.

decisions.choice: single quote closes Yahweh's words; double quote closes Gad's speech
decisions.reason: Gad's own question at the end is not part of Yahweh's message, so the single quote closes before it.

decisions.choice: a plague (Balanced); a deadly plague (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:13: Literal keeps "pestilence" for this word and "plague" for the different word in verses 17 and 22; Balanced and Readable use the everyday word "plague".

decisions.choice: three days when the LORD will strike with his own sword. That would be ...
decisions.reason: Readable says what "three days of the sword of the LORD" means and starts a new sentence for the pestilence and the angel, which describe that third choice. The pronoun "his" here refers to God.

records.source: וַיֹּ֧אמֶר דָּוִ֛יד אֶל־גָּ֖ד צַר־לִ֣י מְאֹ֑ד אֶפְּלָה־נָּ֣א בְיַד־יְהוָ֗ה כִּֽי־רַבִּ֤ים רַחֲמָיו֙ מְאֹ֔ד וּבְיַד־אָדָ֖ם אַל־אֶפֹּֽל׃
records.gloss: And said David to Gad, [It is] distress to me exceedingly. Let me fall, please, into [the] hand of Yahweh, for great [are] his mercies exceedingly; but into [the] hand of man let me not fall.
pieces: David said to Gad, "I am in deep distress. Let me fall into the hand of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mercy is very great; but do not let me fall into human hands."

L.13: And David said to Gad, "[It is] very distressing to me. Let me fall, please, into the hand of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mercies [are] very great; but into the hand of man let me not fall."

R.13: David answered Gad, "This is a terrible choice! Let it be {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} who punishes me, because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is very merciful. But do not let me fall into the power of human beings."

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:14
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:14 has "let us fall", with David speaking for the whole people, and "his mercies are great". Here David says "let me fall" both times, and adds "very" to Yahweh's mercies.

decisions.choice: fall into the hand of: come under the power of
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:14. "Hand" stands for power. David would rather be punished directly by Yahweh than be handed over to enemies.

decisions.choice: mercies: deep compassion
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:14. The word is plural, for the many acts of Yahweh's compassion; it is the love of a parent for a child (Psalm 103:13).

decisions.choice: This is a terrible choice!; Let it be the LORD who punishes me
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:14: Readable explains the idiom "fall into the hand of" and puts David's distress in plain words. The pronoun "his" in "his mercies" refers to God.

records.source: וַיִּתֵּ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה דֶּ֖בֶר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיִּפֹּל֙ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵ֔ל שִׁבְעִ֥ים אֶ֖לֶף אִֽישׁ׃
records.gloss: And put Yahweh pestilence on Israel; and fell of Israel seventy thousand man.
pieces: So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent a plague on Israel, and 70,000 of the people of Israel died.

L.14: So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent pestilence on Israel, and of Israel 70,000 {{gender:people|men}} fell.

R.14: So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent a plague on Israel, and 70,000 people in Israel died.

decisions.choice: a shorter form of 2 Samuel 24:15
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:15 adds that the pestilence lasted "from the morning until the appointed time", and says that "of the people from Dan to Beersheba" 70,000 died. Here the verse says only "of Israel", and uses the verb "fell" for "died".

decisions.choice: 70,000 persons: men and women among the people
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:15: the word usually meaning "man" is used after a number as a counting word for persons. On the number word, see verse 5.

decisions.choice: fell: died
decisions.reason: "Fell" is used of those who die, in battle or by a disaster (1 Samuel 4:10).

decisions.choice: people (default); men (alternative)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:15: the Hebrew word here counts persons of both sexes, so Literal uses the gender setting.

decisions.choice: a plague; died
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:15: Balanced and Readable use the everyday word "plague" and say "died" for "fell".

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַח֩ הָאֱלֹהִ֨ים׀מַלְאָ֥ךְ׀לִֽירוּשָׁלִַם֮ לְהַשְׁחִיתָהּ֒ וּכְהַשְׁחִ֗ית רָאָ֤ה יְהוָה֙ וַיִּנָּ֣חֶם עַל־הָֽרָעָ֔ה וַיֹּ֨אמֶר לַמַּלְאָ֤ךְ הַמַּשְׁחִית֙ רַ֔ב עַתָּ֖ה הֶ֣רֶף יָדֶ֑ךָ וּמַלְאַ֤ךְ יְהוָה֙ עֹמֵ֔ד עִם־גֹּ֖רֶן אָרְנָ֥ן הַיְבוּסִֽי׃ס
records.gloss: And sent God an angel to Jerusalem to destroy it; and as [he was] destroying, saw Yahweh and relented concerning the harm, and said to the angel destroying, Enough! Now let drop your hand. And [the] angel of Yahweh [was] standing by [the] threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
pieces: Then God sent an angel to Jerusalem to destroy it. But as the angel was bringing destruction, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} saw it and relented from the disaster. He said to the angel who was bringing destruction, "Enough! Now hold back your hand." The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was then standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

L.15: And God sent an angel to Jerusalem to destroy it; but as he was destroying, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} saw and relented concerning the harm, and said to the angel who was destroying, "Enough! Now let your hand drop." And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

R.15: Then God sent an angel to Jerusalem to destroy the city. But while the angel was at work, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} saw what was happening. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} was sorry for the harm being done, so {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} decided to stop it. He said to the angel who was bringing destruction, "That is enough! Stop now!" At that moment the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was standing beside the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. A threshing floor was a flat, open place where grain was beaten out.

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:16
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:16 says "the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it" and that Yahweh spoke to "the angel who was destroying among the people". Here God sends the angel, Yahweh "saw" before he relented, and the angel of Yahweh is "standing" by the threshing floor. The rest is the same. This verse names God both as "God" and as "Yahweh".

decisions.choice: Ornan: the name as Chronicles gives it
decisions.reason: Chronicles calls the owner of the threshing floor Ornan throughout. 2 Samuel 24:16-24 calls him Araunah, and its written Hebrew spells that name in several ways (see the note at 2 Samuel 24:16). Both are probably forms of one Jebusite name, written differently in Hebrew. Each book's form is kept.

decisions.choice: Yahweh saw and relented concerning the harm: he was moved to stop the disaster
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:16. The verb means to be moved with grief or pity and so change course (Exodus 32:14; Jeremiah 18:8). Here Yahweh first "sees" the destruction, and his mercy, which David trusted in (verse 13), stops it.

decisions.choice: the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite: the future site of the temple
decisions.reason: A threshing floor was a hard, flat area on open high ground where the wind carried off the chaff. The Jebusites held Jerusalem before David took it (11:4-6). 2 Chronicles 3:1 says Solomon built the temple on Mount Moriah, "at the place David had prepared, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite".

decisions.choice: was sorry for the harm being done, so he decided to stop it; A threshing floor was ...
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:16: Readable explains "relented" and adds a sentence saying what a threshing floor was.

records.source: וַיִּשָּׂ֨א דָוִ֜יד אֶת־עֵינָ֗יו וַיַּ֞רְא אֶת־מַלְאַ֤ךְ יְהוָה֙ עֹמֵ֗ד בֵּ֤ין הָאָ֨רֶץ֙ וּבֵ֣ין הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וְחַרְבּ֤וֹ שְׁלוּפָה֙ בְּיָד֔וֹ נְטוּיָ֖ה עַל־יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וַיִּפֹּ֨ל דָּוִ֧יד וְהַזְּקֵנִ֛ים מְכֻסִּ֥ים בַּשַּׂקִּ֖ים עַל־פְּנֵיהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And lifted David his eyes and saw [the] angel of Yahweh standing between the earth and between the heavens, and his sword drawn in his hand, stretched out over Jerusalem. And fell David and the elders, covered in sackcloth, on their faces.
pieces: David looked up and saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} standing between earth and heaven, holding in his hand a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem. David and the elders, dressed in sackcloth, fell face down.

L.16: And David lifted up his eyes and saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} standing between the earth and the heavens, with his sword drawn in his hand, stretched out over Jerusalem. And David and the elders, covered in sackcloth, fell on their faces.

R.16: David looked up and saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} standing between earth and heaven. The angel had a sword in his hand, held out over Jerusalem. Then David and the leaders of Israel bowed down with their faces to the ground. They were dressed in sackcloth, rough cloth that people wore to show grief and sorrow for sin.

decisions.choice: the angel with a drawn sword: a scene not in 2 Samuel 24
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:17 says only that David saw the angel striking the people. Here David sees the angel standing in the air with his sword drawn over the city, as Balaam saw the angel of Yahweh "with his sword drawn in his hand" (Numbers 22:23, 31) and Joshua saw the commander of Yahweh's army (Joshua 5:13). The elders in sackcloth are also not in 2 Samuel.

decisions.choice: between the earth and the heavens: in the air, above the city
decisions.reason: The phrase places the angel in plain sight, between ground and sky (Absalom hung "between heaven and earth" in 2 Samuel 18:9). The heavens here are the sky above.

decisions.choice: the elders covered in sackcloth fell on their faces: mourning and repentance
decisions.reason: Sackcloth was a coarse cloth, often of goat hair, worn in grief and in repentance (Genesis 37:34; 1 Kings 21:27). The elders were the leading men of the people. Falling face down was the posture of one pleading before God (Numbers 16:22).

decisions.choice: the leaders of Israel; bowed down with their faces to the ground; rough cloth that people wore to show grief and sorrow for sin
decisions.reason: Readable says "leaders" for elders, explains "fell on their faces", and adds a sentence saying what sackcloth was and why it was worn.

decisions.choice: dressed in sackcloth; fell face down
decisions.reason: Balanced puts "covered in" and "on their faces" in everyday words.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֣יד אֶֽל־הָאֱלֹהִ֡ים הֲלֹא֩ אֲנִ֨י אָמַ֜רְתִּי לִמְנ֣וֹת בָּעָ֗ם וַאֲנִי־ה֤וּא אֲשֶׁר־חָטָ֨אתִי֙ וְהָרֵ֣עַ הֲרֵע֔וֹתִי וְאֵ֥לֶּה הַצֹּ֖אן מֶ֣ה עָשׂ֑וּ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהַ֗י תְּהִ֨י נָ֤א יָֽדְךָ֙ בִּ֚י וּבְבֵ֣ית אָבִ֔י וּֽבְעַמְּךָ֖ לֹ֥א לְמַגֵּפָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And said David to God, [Was it] not I [who] said to count the people? And I [am] he who sinned and did great evil; and these, the sheep, what have they done? Yahweh my God, let be, please, your hand on me and on [the] house of my father, but on your people not for a plague.
pieces: David said to God, "Did I not give the command to count the people? It is I who have sinned and done great wrong. But these sheep, what have they done? {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}} my God, please let {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} hand be against me and my father's family, but do not let this plague strike {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people."

L.17: And David said to God, "Was it not I who said to count the people? I am the one who has sinned and done great wrong; but these sheep, what have they done? {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}} my God, please let {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} hand be against me and against my father's house, but not against {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people with a plague."

R.17: David said to God, "It was my order to count the people! I am the one who sinned and did this terrible wrong. These people are like sheep. What have they done to deserve this? {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}} my God, please punish me and my family instead. Do not let the plague go on striking {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people."

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:17
decisions.reason: In 2 Samuel 24:17 David speaks to Yahweh "when he saw the angel who was striking the people", and begins "Look, I have sinned". Here he speaks to God, begins with the question "Was it not I who said to count the people?", strengthens "done wrong" with a doubled verb, calls on "Yahweh my God", and adds a last request: "but not against your people with a plague".

decisions.choice: Was it not I ... I am the one who: David puts the blame on himself
decisions.reason: The question expects "yes": the order was his. The pronoun "I" is added before the verbs, and the verb "done wrong" is doubled, which stresses that the guilt is David's, not the people's.

decisions.choice: these sheep: the people in David's care
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:17. David was called to shepherd Yahweh's people (11:2), and he now sees them as a flock suffering for their shepherd's fault.

decisions.choice: let your hand be against me and my father's house: punish me and my family
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:17. "Hand" stands for power used in judgment; "my father's house" is David's own family line.

decisions.choice: It was my order to count the people!; These people are like sheep; to deserve this; punish me and my family instead
decisions.reason: Readable turns the first question into the statement it implies, explains the picture of the sheep and puts "let your hand be against" in plain words, as at 2 Samuel 24:17.

records.source: וּמַלְאַ֧ךְ יְהוָ֛ה אָמַ֥ר אֶל־גָּ֖ד לֵאמֹ֣ר לְדָוִ֑יד כִּ֣י׀יַעֲלֶ֣ה דָוִ֗יד לְהָקִ֤ים מִזְבֵּ֨חַ֙ לַיהוָ֔ה בְּגֹ֖רֶן אָרְנָ֥ן הַיְבֻסִֽי׃
records.gloss: And [the] angel of Yahweh said to Gad to say to David that should go up David to set up an altar to Yahweh on [the] threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
pieces: Then the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told Gad to tell David to go up and set up an altar for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

L.18: And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told Gad to say to David that David should go up and raise an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

R.18: Then the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told Gad to give David this message: "Go up to the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Build an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} there."

decisions.choice: the angel gives the command through Gad: a difference from 2 Samuel 24:18
decisions.reason: In 2 Samuel 24:18 Gad simply comes to David "on that day" and tells him, "Go up, raise an altar." Here the angel of Yahweh tells Gad what to say, and the command is given as reported speech. The words for the altar and the place are the same.

decisions.choice: go up: the threshing floor lay higher than David's city
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:18. The threshing floor was on the hill north of the city of David, where Solomon later built the temple (2 Chronicles 3:1).

decisions.choice: raise an altar: the place where the angel stood becomes a place of sacrifice
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:18. The altar is to stand where the angel of Yahweh stood (verse 15). Yahweh himself names the place of worship (Deuteronomy 12:5).

decisions.choice: told Gad to give David this message: "Go up ... Build an altar ... there."
decisions.reason: Readable turns the reported command into direct speech, names the place first and splits the command into two sentences, as at 2 Samuel 24:18.

records.heading: David buys Ornan's threshing floor

records.source: וַיַּ֤עַל דָּוִיד֙ בִּדְבַר־גָּ֔ד אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבֶּ֖ר בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And went up David at [the] word of Gad which he spoke in [the] name of Yahweh.
pieces: So David went up as Gad had told him in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.19: So David went up at the word of Gad, which he had spoken in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.19: So David went up, doing what Gad had told him. Gad had given him this message with the authority of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: in the name of Yahweh: a difference from 2 Samuel 24:19
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:19 reads "according to the word of Gad, as Yahweh commanded". Here Gad's word is one "he spoke in the name of Yahweh". Both make the same point: the prophet's word was Yahweh's command.

decisions.choice: spoke in the name of Yahweh: spoke as Yahweh's messenger, with his authority
decisions.reason: A prophet who speaks "in the name of Yahweh" speaks for him (Deuteronomy 18:19-22).

decisions.choice: with the authority of the LORD
decisions.reason: Readable explains "in the name of" and gives it its own sentence.

records.source: וַיָּ֣שָׁב אָרְנָ֗ן וַיַּרְא֙ אֶת־הַמַּלְאָ֔ךְ וְאַרְבַּ֧עַת בָּנָ֛יו עִמּ֖וֹ מִֽתְחַבְּאִ֑ים וְאָרְנָ֖ן דָּ֥שׁ חִטִּֽים׃
records.gloss: And turned Ornan and saw the angel, and four sons of his with him hiding themselves; and Ornan [was] threshing wheat.
pieces: Ornan turned and saw the angel, and the four sons with him hid themselves. Ornan had been threshing wheat.

L.20: And Ornan turned and saw the angel, and his four sons who were with him hid themselves. Now Ornan was threshing wheat.

R.20: Ornan was threshing wheat at the time. He turned around and saw the angel. His four sons, who were there with him, hid themselves.

decisions.choice: Ornan sees the angel: a difference from 2 Samuel 24:20
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:20 says that Araunah "looked down and saw the king and his servants coming over toward him". Here Ornan turns and sees the angel, his four sons hide, and he is threshing wheat; none of this is in 2 Samuel. In Hebrew the words for "the angel" and "the king" differ by a single letter, and the verbs "turned" and "looked down" are not far apart either, so the two accounts may go back to one text read in two ways. As the text stands, Ornan sees the angel first and David in the next verse.

decisions.choice: hiding; was threshing: what was going on when Ornan saw the angel
decisions.reason: Both verbs describe an action under way. The sons hid as soon as the angel was seen, and Ornan was in the middle of his work, so the threshing floor was in use at harvest time.

decisions.choice: Ornan was threshing wheat at the time.
decisions.reason: Readable puts the background first, so the reader knows where Ornan was before he sees the angel.

decisions.choice: had been threshing
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "had been" because the clause gives the background to what Ornan saw.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֥א דָוִ֖יד עַד־אָרְנָ֑ן וַיַּבֵּ֤ט אָרְנָן֙ וַיַּ֣רְא אֶת־דָּוִ֔יד וַיֵּצֵא֙ מִן־הַגֹּ֔רֶן וַיִּשְׁתַּ֧חוּ לְדָוִ֛יד אַפַּ֖יִם אָֽרְצָה׃
records.gloss: And came David to Ornan; and looked Ornan and saw David, and went out from the threshing floor and bowed down to David [with] face to [the] ground.
pieces: When David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David. He went out from the threshing floor and bowed before David with his face to the ground.

L.21: And David came to Ornan. And Ornan looked and saw David, and he went out from the threshing floor and bowed down to David [with his] face to the ground.

R.21: David came to Ornan. When Ornan looked up and saw David, he left the threshing floor. He bowed down in front of David with his face to the ground.

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:20
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:20 has Araunah "look down" and see "the king and his servants" coming toward him, and go out to bow before "the king". Here David comes alone in the telling, Ornan "looks" (a different verb), and he goes out "from the threshing floor" to bow before "David".

decisions.choice: bowed down with his face to the ground: the full honor given to a king
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:20. This deep bow, lying face down, was how a subject greeted a king.

decisions.choice: [with his] face
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has only "face to the ground"; Literal supplies the words English needs in brackets.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר דָּוִ֜יד אֶל־אָרְנָ֗ן תְּנָה־לִּי֙ מְק֣וֹם הַגֹּ֔רֶן וְאֶבְנֶה־בּ֥וֹ מִזְבֵּ֖חַ לַיהוָ֑ה בְּכֶ֤סֶף מָלֵא֙ תְּנֵ֣הוּ לִ֔י וְתֵעָצַ֥ר הַמַּגֵּפָ֖ה מֵעַ֥ל הָעָֽם׃
records.gloss: And said David to Ornan, Give to me [the] place of the threshing floor, and I will build on it an altar to Yahweh; for full silver give it to me, and may be held back the plague from on the people.
pieces: David said to Ornan, "Let me have the site of this threshing floor so that I can build an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} on it. Sell it to me at its full price, so that the plague on the people may be stopped."

L.22: And David said to Ornan, "Give me the site of the threshing floor, so that I may build on it an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Give it to me for the full price, so that the plague may be held back from the people."

R.22: David said to Ornan, "Let me have your threshing floor. I want to build an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} on it. Sell it to me at the full price, so that the plague on the people will stop."

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:21
decisions.reason: In 2 Samuel 24:21 Araunah first asks why the king has come, and David answers, "To buy the threshing floor from you, to build an altar to Yahweh, so that the plague may be held back from the people." Here Ornan asks nothing; David speaks first and asks for "the place" of the threshing floor "for the full price". The purpose, that the plague may be held back, is the same.

decisions.choice: for the full price: as Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah
decisions.reason: Abraham asked to buy his burial place "for the full price" with the same words (Genesis 23:9). David, like Abraham, insists on a fair purchase so that the place will be truly his.

decisions.choice: the place: the site, the ground itself
decisions.reason: The word means a place or site, and is often used of a place set apart for worship (Deuteronomy 12:5). David asks for the whole site, not only the use of it; verse 25 names the price "for the place".

decisions.choice: may be held back: may be stopped
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:21. The same verb is used when the plague was stopped after Aaron made atonement (Numbers 17:13, 15).

decisions.choice: Let me have; Sell it to me
decisions.reason: The verb "give" in a sale means to hand over for payment. Balanced and Readable say "let me have" and "sell" so the reader does not think David is asking for a gift.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אָרְנָ֤ן אֶל־דָּוִיד֙ קַֽח־לָ֔ךְ וְיַ֛עַשׂ אֲדֹנִ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ הַטּ֣וֹב בְּעֵינָ֑יו רְאֵה֩ נָתַ֨תִּי הַבָּקָ֜ר לָֽעֹל֗וֹת וְהַמּוֹרִגִּ֧ים לָעֵצִ֛ים וְהַחִטִּ֥ים לַמִּנְחָ֖ה הַכֹּ֥ל נָתָֽתִּי׃
records.gloss: And said Ornan to David, Take for yourself, and let do my lord the king the good in his eyes; see, I give the oxen for the burnt offerings, and the threshing sledges for the wood, and the wheat for the grain offering; the whole I give.
pieces: Ornan said to David, "Take it, and let my lord the king do whatever he thinks best. Look, I am giving you the oxen for burnt offerings, the threshing sledges for firewood, and the wheat for a grain offering. I give it all."

L.23: And Ornan said to David, "Take [it] for yourself, and let my lord the king do what [is] good in his eyes. See, I give the oxen for the burnt offerings, and the threshing sledges for the wood, and the wheat for the grain offering. I give it all."

R.23: Ornan said to David, "Take it, my king, and do whatever you want with it. Here, I will give you the oxen for the burnt offerings. You can use the wooden threshing sledges as firewood. And here is wheat for the grain offering. I give you all of it."

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:22-23
decisions.reason: In 2 Samuel 24:22-23 Araunah says, "Let my lord the king take and offer up what is good in his eyes", offers "the threshing sledges and the equipment of the oxen" for the wood, ends "All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king", and blesses David: "May Yahweh your God accept you." Here Ornan says "take it for yourself" and "let him do", leaves out the oxen's equipment, adds the wheat for the grain offering, ends simply "I give it all", and gives no blessing.

decisions.choice: I give: an offer made by the words themselves
decisions.reason: The verb form usually tells of a completed act ("I have given"). Used in an offer like this, it means "I hereby give": the gift is made as Ornan speaks (compare Genesis 23:11).

decisions.choice: threshing sledges; wheat for the grain offering
decisions.reason: A threshing sledge was a heavy wooden board with sharp stones set into its underside, dragged over the grain (Isaiah 41:15); its wood could be burned. The wheat Ornan was threshing (verse 20) could supply flour for a grain offering, which went with burnt offerings (Numbers 15:1-10).

decisions.choice: my king; You can use the wooden threshing sledges as firewood; And here is wheat
decisions.reason: Readable lets Ornan speak to the king directly and says plainly what the wood and wheat are for, as at 2 Samuel 24:22.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ דָּוִיד֙ לְאָרְנָ֔ן לֹ֕א כִּֽי־קָנֹ֥ה אֶקְנֶ֖ה בְּכֶ֣סֶף מָלֵ֑א כִּ֠י לֹא־אֶשָּׂ֤א אֲשֶׁר־לְךָ֙ לַיהוָ֔ה וְהַעֲל֥וֹת עוֹלָ֖ה חִנָּֽם׃
records.gloss: And said the king David to Ornan, No, for buying I will buy [it] for full silver; for not I will take what [is] to you for Yahweh, and offer up a burnt offering without cost.
pieces: But King David said to Ornan, "No, I insist on paying you the full price for it. I will not take what is yours for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, or offer a burnt offering at no cost to myself."

L.24: But King David said to Ornan, "No, I will surely buy [it] for the full price; for I will not take what [is] yours for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and offer up a burnt offering without cost."

R.24: But King David answered Ornan, "No, I will pay you the full price for it. I will not take what belongs to you and give it to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I will not give a burnt offering that I got for free."

decisions.choice: differences from 2 Samuel 24:24
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:24 has "the king", "I will surely buy it from you for a price", and "I will not offer up to Yahweh my God burnt offerings without cost", and then tells of the purchase in the same verse. Here he is "King David", the price is "the full price", he adds "I will not take what is yours for Yahweh", speaks of one burnt offering, and the payment is told in the next verse.

decisions.choice: I will surely buy: David insists
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:24, the verb is doubled for emphasis. David will not accept the gift.

decisions.choice: a burnt offering without cost: a sacrifice must cost the one who offers it
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:24. An offering made from someone else's property would not be David's own gift.

decisions.choice: at no cost to myself (Balanced); that I got for free (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:24: the Hebrew word means "for nothing, without payment", and the wording makes clear that the cost is David's.

records.source: וַיִּתֵּ֥ן דָּוִ֛יד לְאָרְנָ֖ן בַּמָּק֑וֹם שִׁקְלֵ֣י זָהָ֔ב מִשְׁקָ֖ל שֵׁ֥שׁ מֵאֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And gave David to Ornan for the place shekels of gold, [a] weight [of] six hundred.
pieces: So David paid Ornan {{units:about 15 pounds of gold|600 shekels of gold}} by weight for the site.

L.25: So David gave Ornan for the site 600 shekels of gold by weight.

R.25: So David paid Ornan {{units:about 15 pounds of gold|600 shekels of gold}} for the land.

decisions.choice: 600 shekels of gold for the site: the price in this account
decisions.reason: 2 Samuel 24:24 says David bought "the threshing floor and the oxen" for 50 shekels of silver. Here he pays 600 shekels of gold "for the place". The two figures may refer to different purchases, the smaller to the threshing floor and the oxen, the larger to the whole site on which the temple was later built (22:1; 2 Chronicles 3:1); or the difference may come from the way the story was passed down. The text does not explain it.

decisions.choice: shekels by weight: gold weighed out, not coins
decisions.reason: Payment was made in metal by weight; a shekel was a weight of about 2/5 ounce. "By weight" stresses that the full amount was weighed out.

decisions.choice: about 15 pounds of gold (default); 600 shekels of gold (alternative)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the modern weight with the shekel as the alternative. Literal keeps the Hebrew unit.

decisions.choice: the land
decisions.reason: Readable says "the land" for "the place", the whole site David bought.

records.source: וַיִּבֶן֩ שָׁ֨ם דָּוִ֤יד מִזְבֵּ֨חַ֙ לַיהוָ֔ה וַיַּ֥עַל עֹל֖וֹת וּשְׁלָמִ֑ים וַיִּקְרָא֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֔ה וַיַּֽעֲנֵ֤הוּ בָאֵשׁ֙ מִן־הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם עַ֖ל מִזְבַּ֥ח הָעֹלָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And built there David an altar to Yahweh and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings; and called to Yahweh, and he answered him with fire from the heavens on [the] altar of the burnt offering.
pieces: David built an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} there and sacrificed burnt offerings and peace offerings. He called on {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} answered him by sending fire from heaven onto the altar of burnt offering.

L.26: And David built there an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings. And he called on {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} answered him with fire from the heavens on the altar of burnt offering.

R.26: David built an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} there. He offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on it. He prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} answered him. He sent fire from heaven down onto the altar of burnt offering.

decisions.choice: David calls and Yahweh answers with fire: a difference from 2 Samuel 24:25
decisions.reason: The first half of the verse is the same as 2 Samuel 24:25. There the story ends: "Yahweh was entreated for the land, and the plague was held back from Israel." Here David calls on Yahweh and Yahweh answers with fire from heaven; the end of the plague is told in the next verse.

decisions.choice: fire from heaven on the altar: Yahweh accepts the sacrifice and the place
decisions.reason: Fire from Yahweh fell on the burnt offering when the tabernacle's altar was first used (Leviticus 9:24), and on Elijah's offering on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:38). It will fall again when Solomon dedicates the temple on this site (2 Chronicles 7:1). The fire shows that Yahweh accepts the offering and has chosen this altar.

decisions.choice: burnt offerings and peace offerings
decisions.reason: As in 2 Samuel 24:25. A burnt offering was given wholly to Yahweh on the altar; a peace offering was shared in a meal by the worshipers (Leviticus 1; 3).

decisions.choice: the LORD answered him
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "he answered him". Balanced and Readable name the LORD so the two men are not confused.

decisions.choice: prayed to (Readable); by sending fire (Balanced); He sent fire ... down onto (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says "prayed" for "called on". Balanced and Readable supply "sending" or "sent" to show how the fire came.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ לַמַּלְאָ֔ךְ וַיָּ֥שֶׁב חַרְבּ֖וֹ אֶל־נְדָנָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And said Yahweh to the angel, and he returned his sword to its sheath.
pieces: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave the angel a command, and the angel put his sword back into its sheath.

L.27: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to the angel, and he put his sword back into its sheath.

R.27: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave an order to the angel, and the angel put his sword away.

decisions.choice: the angel sheathes his sword: a verse not in 2 Samuel 24
decisions.reason: In 2 Samuel 24:16 Yahweh tells the angel, "Now let your hand drop", and the story does not mention a sword. Here the sword David saw drawn over Jerusalem (verse 16) goes back into its sheath, and so the judgment is over.

decisions.choice: spoke to: gave an order to
decisions.reason: The verb is the ordinary word for "said"; what Yahweh says to the angel is a command, as the angel's obedience shows.

decisions.choice: gave the angel a command; the angel put his sword back
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what kind of speaking this was and name the angel as the one who put the sword away.

records.source: בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֔יא בִּרְא֤וֹת דָּוִיד֙ כִּי־עָנָ֣הוּ יְהוָ֔ה בְּגֹ֖רֶן אָרְנָ֣ן הַיְבוּסִ֑י וַיִּזְבַּ֖ח שָֽׁם׃
records.gloss: At the time the that, when saw David that had answered him Yahweh at [the] threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, and he sacrificed there.
pieces: At that time, when David saw that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had given him an answer at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he offered his sacrifices there.

L.28: At that time, when David saw that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had answered him at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he sacrificed there.

R.28: David saw that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had answered his prayer at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. So at that time he offered sacrifices there.

decisions.choice: verses 28-30: the Chronicler's own comment, not in 2 Samuel 24
decisions.reason: Here the story stops and the writer explains why David went on offering sacrifices at Ornan's threshing floor rather than at the tabernacle. The explanation leads to David's words in 22:1: "This is the house of Yahweh God, and this is the altar of burnt offering for Israel."

decisions.choice: at that time ... he sacrificed there: David's sacrifices after the answer
decisions.reason: "At that time" ties the sentence to the fire from heaven (verse 26). Seeing that Yahweh had answered him at that place, David made it his place of sacrifice.

decisions.choice: offered sacrifices; given him an answer (Balanced); answered his prayer (Readable)
decisions.reason: The verb means to slaughter animals in sacrifice. Balanced and Readable use the usual English phrase. Readable says what Yahweh answered: David's call in verse 26.

decisions.choice: David saw ... So at that time ...
decisions.reason: Readable puts the cause in its own sentence first.

records.source: וּמִשְׁכַּ֣ן יְ֠הוָה אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֨ה מֹשֶׁ֧ה בַמִּדְבָּ֛ר וּמִזְבַּ֥ח הָעוֹלָ֖ה בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֑יא בַּבָּמָ֖ה בְּגִבְעֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And [the] tabernacle of Yahweh which made Moses in the wilderness, and [the] altar of the burnt offering, [were] at the time the that in [the] high place at Gibeon.
pieces: Now at that time the tabernacle of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, made by Moses in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering were at the high place in Gibeon.

L.29: Now the tabernacle of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, which Moses made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering [were] at that time at the high place at Gibeon.

R.29: At that time the tabernacle of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the tent that Moses had made in the wilderness, was at the hilltop shrine in Gibeon. The altar for burnt offerings was there too.

decisions.choice: the tabernacle at Gibeon: where the official worship took place
decisions.reason: 1 Chronicles 16:39-40 says David left the priest Zadok at the tabernacle at the high place in Gibeon to offer the daily burnt offerings, while the ark was in Jerusalem. Solomon went there to sacrifice at the start of his reign (1 Kings 3:4; 2 Chronicles 1:3-6). This verse is not in 2 Samuel 24.

decisions.choice: the high place at Gibeon: a hilltop place of worship a few miles northwest of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: A high place was a raised site for worship. Gibeon was a town of Benjamin (Joshua 18:25). Here the high place is the lawful site of the tabernacle, not a pagan shrine.

decisions.choice: Now the tabernacle ...: background that explains verse 28
decisions.reason: The sentence begins with its subject, not with a verb, which marks it as an explanation set beside the story. It tells why David's sacrifice at Ornan's threshing floor needs explaining: the lawful altar was at Gibeon.

decisions.choice: the tent that Moses had made; the hilltop shrine
decisions.reason: Readable explains "tabernacle" as a tent and says "hilltop shrine" for "high place", as elsewhere in these books.

records.source: וְלֹא־יָכֹ֥ל דָּוִ֛יד לָלֶ֥כֶת לְפָנָ֖יו לִדְרֹ֣שׁ אֱלֹהִ֑ים כִּ֣י נִבְעַ֔ת מִפְּנֵ֕י חֶ֖רֶב מַלְאַ֥ךְ יְהוָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And not was able David to go before it to seek God, for he was terrified from before [the] sword of [the] angel of Yahweh.
pieces: But David could not go there to seek God, because he was terrified of the sword of the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.30: But David could not go before it to seek God, for he was terrified because of the sword of the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.30: But David could not go there to ask God for help, because he was afraid of the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and his sword.

decisions.choice: David afraid of the angel's sword: not in 2 Samuel 24
decisions.reason: This explanation is the Chronicler's own. The sword is the one David saw drawn over Jerusalem (verse 16).

decisions.choice: to seek God: to turn to God in worship and ask his will
decisions.reason: "Seek" is a key word in Chronicles for turning to God in trust and worship (10:13-14; 13:3). David could not go to Gibeon to do this, so he worshiped where God had answered him.

decisions.choice: go before it: go to the tabernacle and its altar at Gibeon
decisions.reason: "It" points back to the tabernacle and altar of verse 29. The text does not say exactly why fear of the angel kept David from the journey; it may be that he did not dare leave the place where the angel had stopped, or that the terror still held him.

decisions.choice: go there
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "go there" for "go before it": to the tabernacle at Gibeon.

decisions.choice: to ask God for help
decisions.reason: Readable says what seeking God means in plain words, as at 10:14.
